blocks.text: **You are a medical student in the antenatal clinic. Take an obstetric history from this 28-year-old pregnant woman.**
**Take a focused obstetric history from this patient who presents with vaginal bleeding in pregnancy.**
**A 32-year-old G3P2 at 34 weeks' gestation presents with reduced fetal movements. Take an appropriate history.**
The important point is that **the structure remains similar**, but you must adapt the history to the presenting complaint.
A good obstetric history can be remembered as:

**P** — Presenting complaint
**A** — Antenatal history/current pregnancy
**P** — Previous obstetric history
**P** — Previous pregnancy complications
**P** — Past gynaecological history
**P** — Past medical/surgical history
**S** — Social/family/drug history
**M** — Management plan / summary
But for an OSCE, I prefer this practical sequence:

**Introduction → Presenting complaint → Current pregnancy → Previous pregnancies → Gynaecological history → Medical/surgical history → Drugs/allergies → Family history → Social history → Summary → Examination/investigations/plan**
"Good morning. My name is Dr ___, I'm one of the doctors looking after you."
"Could I confirm your name and age, please?"
"I'd like to ask you some questions about your pregnancy and your previous pregnancies. This will help me understand your current pregnancy and make sure we identify any potential problems."

items.text: Use a professional but empathetic tone.

blocks.text: Don't simply accept the patient's estimate.
"When was the first day of your last menstrual period?"
Then establish whether the pregnancy has been dated by ultrasound.
**"What brought you to the hospital today?"**
Allow the woman to explain without immediately interrupting.
"When did you first notice the leakage?"

items.text: When movements were last felt normally

blocks.text: This is one of the **highest-yield parts** of the station.
The examiner wants to know whether this pregnancy has been normal or high-risk.
Calculate the expected date of delivery.
However, if an early dating ultrasound is available, use the documented dating appropriately.
"How did you first know you were pregnant?"
"When did you first register for antenatal care?"

items.text: How many weeks pregnant were you?
Was this your first antenatal visit?

blocks.text: "How regularly have you been attending antenatal clinic?"

items.text: Any abnormal findings at previous visits

blocks.text: "Has anyone told you that your blood pressure was high?"
"Have you been told that you are anaemic?"
"Have you been told that you have diabetes?"
"Have there been any concerns about the baby's growth?"
"Have you ever been admitted during this pregnancy?"
Ask what investigations she has had.
"When did you first start feeling the baby move?"
"How have the baby's movements been recently?"
If the patient presents because of reduced movements:
"When was the last time you felt the baby move normally?"
Do **not** accept vague reassurance such as:
Clarify the change from the patient's normal pattern.
This is a **very important OSCE area**.
"Any blurring of vision or seeing flashing lights?"
"Any pain in the upper abdomen, particularly under the right ribs?"
"Any sudden swelling of your face or hands?"
"Have you ever been told your blood pressure was high?"
"Have you been unusually tired or weak?"
"Have you had shortness of breath or palpitations?"
**"Have you taken any herbal preparations or traditional medicines during this pregnancy?"**
"Do you have any allergies to medications or anything else?"
This is another major scoring area.

content_groups.group_title: Year → Gestational age → Outcome → Mode of delivery → Baby → Complications

blocks.text: "I'd like to ask you about each of your previous pregnancies."
"How many weeks were you when you delivered?"
"Was the delivery vaginal or by caesarean section?"
"Did you have any complications during pregnancy, labour or after delivery?"
This is much better than simply asking:
Because patients may forget important events.
"How many caesarean sections have you had?"
"Do you know what type of incision was made?"

blocks.title: Then determine whether she has had:

blocks.text: This becomes particularly important when discussing **mode of delivery in the current pregnancy**.
"Have you ever had a pregnancy that did not continue to term?"
Even though this is an obstetric history, important gynaecological history is relevant.
This should be asked **professionally and sensitively**.
"I ask these questions routinely because they can affect pregnancy and reproductive health."
"Have you ever been admitted to hospital for any serious illness?"
"Have you ever had surgery on your uterus?"
This can dramatically alter obstetric management.
"Are there twins in either your family or your partner's family?"
"Do you smoke or use any tobacco products?"
This can be an important OSCE differentiator.
If appropriate, ensure the woman is **alone and safe** before asking.
"I ask all pregnant women this routinely: do you ever feel frightened or unsafe at home?"
"Has anyone forced you to have sexual contact against your wishes?"
A focused review should cover important pregnancy complications.
This is where many candidates lose marks.

"This is a 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 34 weeks' gestation by a reliable LMP, with dating confirmed by an early ultrasound. She booked for antenatal care at 10 weeks and has attended regularly. The current pregnancy has been uncomplicated apart from mild iron-deficiency anaemia. She reports normal fetal movements and denies vaginal bleeding, leakage of fluid, contractions, headache, visual disturbance or epigastric pain."
"Her previous pregnancy was delivered at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery with no significant maternal or neonatal complications."
"She has no significant medical or surgical history, takes routine antenatal supplements and has no known drug allergies."
"There are no significant family or social risk factors identified."
"I would now like to examine her and review her antenatal records and relevant investigations."
The summary should **highlight the risk factor**, rather than bury it.

"This is a 30-year-old G3P1+1 at 32 weeks' gestation with a previous pregnancy complicated by severe pre-eclampsia requiring preterm delivery at 32 weeks. The current pregnancy has been appropriately booked and she is currently asymptomatic with no headache, visual disturbance or epigastric pain."

"This is a 29-year-old G2P1 at 38 weeks' gestation with one previous caesarean section for failure to progress. The current pregnancy has been uncomplicated, and she is currently being assessed regarding mode of delivery."

"This is a 27-year-old G2P1 at 36 weeks' gestation presenting with a reduction in fetal movements since this morning. There is no associated vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, abdominal pain or uterine contraction."
That immediately tells the examiner **what the clinical problem is**.

subsections.subsection_title: 33. WHAT DO YOU DO AFTER THE HISTORY?

blocks.text: "I would assess the mother's immediate clinical condition, perform an appropriate obstetric examination, review her antenatal records, and arrange relevant investigations based on the presenting complaint and gestational age."

items.text: Avoid inappropriate digital vaginal examination if placenta praevia has not been excluded in relevant circumstances

blocks.text: Gravida refers to the total number of times a woman has been pregnant, irrespective of the outcome.
Parity refers to the number of pregnancies reaching the threshold of viability, regardless of whether the infant was born alive or stillborn.
The woman has been pregnant three times and has had two pregnancies reaching the relevant gestational threshold for parity.
This depends on the parity notation being used.
Always clarify the local parity convention if necessary.

content_groups.group_title: Trap 1: Asking only about the current pregnancy

blocks.text: **Current pregnancy + previous pregnancies + medical/gynaecological risk factors.**
Always ask about previous deliveries and their modes.
"I ask all my patients about previous infections because some infections can affect pregnancy. Have you ever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection?"

Don't treat **obstetric history taking** as a list of questions.
**Maternal disease → Previous obstetric problems → Current pregnancy complications → Fetal problems → Social/safeguarding risks.**
That approach makes your history sound much more like a **doctor's clinical assessment** rather than a memorised questionnaire.
